name: Franziskanerkloster Schwaz
kurzbeschreibung: Endowed in 1507 by Maximilian I., Franziskanerkloster Schwaz houses a world-famous Gothic cloister featuring 22 monumental passion frescoes.
beschreibung:
Overview

The Franziskanerkloster Schwaz in the historic silver town of Schwaz in the Tyrolean Unterinntal is a sacred monument and cultural landmark of outstanding European importance. Situated on Gilmstraße at the foot of the Kellerjoch, the Late Gothic monastery complex provides a sanctuary of reflective tranquility amidst the urban townscape. Famous far beyond the borders of Tyrol, the monastery is renowned for its masterful Gothic cloister, which houses one of the most significant and best-preserved monumental passion cycles in all of Central Europe.

History & Art Treasures

In the early 16th century, Schwaz experienced unprecedented economic prosperity fueled by silver and copper mining, rising to become the second-largest city in the Habsburg Empire. To provide pastoral care for the thousands of miners and migrant workers, future Emperor Maximilian I. endowed the monastery in 1507 for the mendicant Franciscan Order. The cloister and the Bonaventura Chapel were consecrated as early as 1509; the three-aisled monastery church of St. Franziskus was completed in 1515. The art-historical crown jewel is the cloister spanning over 200 m²: between 1512 and 1526, an artist whose name remains unrecorded – acclaimed in art history as the Meister des Schwazer Kreuzgangs – created a monumental passion cycle across 22 large wall panels. The paintings closely follow woodcut models by famous contemporaries such as Albrecht Dürer, Martin Schongauer, and Hans Schäufelein. Their distinctiveness lies in the subtle technique: underdrawings were executed with fine quills and then colored with delicate glazes, lending the frescoes the distinct character of oversized woodcuts. Furthermore, the murals vividly reflect the Renaissance era: biblical soldiers appear as contemporary lansquenets with halberds, Schwaz miners are depicted in intricate detail, and donor coats of arms such as those of the powerful Fieger mining dynasty adorn the vaults. The monastery church also impresses with delicate Rococo stucco, masterfully carved choir stalls from 1735, and a Baroque high altar.

Visit & Getting There

The historic cloister and the monastery church are freely accessible to visitors year-round daily from 08:00 to approx. 18:30 (until 19:00 in summer). Admission to both the cloister and the church is free of charge (donations for the painstaking preservation of the heritage-listed ensemble are warmly welcomed). Cultural guided tours are offered via the Silberregion Karwendel tourism board. Getting there by public transport: take ÖBB or S-Bahn Tirol (lines S4, S5) to Schwaz railway station, and from there walk about ten minutes through the old town to Gilmstraße 1, or take the Schwaz city bus directly to the Klosterkirche stop. By car: Inntalautobahn A12, Schwaz exit; parking is readily available in the nearby Stadtgalerien and Stadtplatz parking garages.

Tips

The monastery entrance, the church, and the cloister are designed without steps and are fully accessible for wheelchair users and strollers. The tranquil atmosphere in the verdant inner courtyard of the cloister invites contemplation and peaceful relaxation following your art viewing. Combine your visit with an exploration of Schwaz's historic old town, the silver mine (Silberbergwerk), and the parish church of Maria Himmelfahrt.
